summary: Extends the File Transfer Protocol so it works over both IPv4 and IPv6 and across network address translators. It adds new commands for specifying data connection addresses and ports. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: The old FTP told the server its address in a form that only worked with the old internet addresses. This update lets it work with both old and new kinds of addresses.

questions: how does ftp work with ipv6
how does ftp work through nat
what is the ftp eprt command
what is the ftp epsv command
subtitle: Two new FTP commands, EPRT and EPSV, let FTP data connections work over IPv6 and through NATs.

tldr.problem: FTP's PORT and PASV commands can only describe 32-bit IPv4 addresses, and the earlier fix in RFC 1639 can fail in a multi-protocol environment.
tldr.mechanism: EPRT sends the network protocol, address and TCP port in one delimited string, while EPSV asks the server to listen and returns only a port number, reusing the control connection's protocol and address.
tldr.outcome: FTP can negotiate IPv4 or IPv6 for the data connection, and EPSV avoids address rewriting by NATs and suits firewalls.

today: RFC 2428 is a Proposed Standard from September 1998, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why FTP Needed Extending
sections.content:
The File Transfer Protocol (RFC 959) can only describe IPv4 data connections, because it assumes network addresses are 32 bits long. With IPv6 (RFC 1883) addresses are no longer 32 bits. RFC 1639 had specified extensions for other network protocols, but its mechanism can fail in a multi-protocol environment.

During the transition between IPv4 and IPv6, FTP needs to negotiate the network protocol for data transfer. This document replaces the commands PORT and PASV with EPRT and EPSV, and the framework can support other network protocols in the future.
sections.eli5: FTP used to say where to connect using a short number format. Newer internet addresses are longer and do not fit, so FTP needed new commands.

sections.title: The EPRT Command
sections.content:
EPRT gives the server an extended address for the data connection: the network protocol, the network address and the TCP port. The format is EPRT<space><d><net-prt><d><net-addr><d><tcp-port><d>. The delimiter <d> MUST be an ASCII character in the range 33 to 126, and | (ASCII 124) is recommended unless it clashes with the address encoding.

net-prt MUST be an IANA address family number. The RFC uses 1 for IPv4 (dotted decimal) and 2 for IPv6 (the string forms from RFC 2373). Examples are EPRT |1|132.235.1.2|6275| and EPRT |2|1080::8:800:200C:417A|5282|.
sections.eli5: EPRT is like telling a delivery person the kind of address system, the address and the door number, all separated by a chosen divider character.

sections.title: EPRT Replies and the 522 Error
sections.content:
On a valid EPRT the server MUST return code 200. The standard errors 500 and 501 cover syntax errors. A new code, 522, means the server does not support the requested network protocol.

The text of a 522 response MUST list the supported protocols as a comma-separated list of address family numbers in parentheses, for example Network protocol not supported, use (1,2). The human-readable text before the parenthesis MUST NOT contain the characters ( or ).
sections.eli5: If the server does not speak the kind of address you used, it replies with a special error and a list of the kinds it does understand.

sections.title: The EPSV Command
sections.content:
EPSV asks a server to listen on a data port and wait for a connection. Its success code MUST be 229, and the text MUST end with (<d><d><d><tcp-port><d>), for example Entering Extended Passive Mode (|||6446|). The first two fields are blank and the third is the port. The data connection uses the same network protocol and address as the control connection.

With no argument the server picks the protocol of the control connection. In proxy FTP that may not suit the other server, so a client can send EPSV <net-prt> to request a protocol. If the returned protocol is not supported by the connecting host, the client MUST send ABOR so the server closes its listening connection. If the server does not support the requested protocol it MUST return 522.
sections.eli5: With EPSV the client says: please open a door and tell me its number. The server answers with just the door number, because the building address is already known.

sections.title: EPSV ALL and Command Usage
sections.content:
When the control and data connections are between the same two machines, EPSV MUST be used. It helps transfers through firewalls and Network Address Translators, because firewalls generally do not allow incoming connections, which EPRT-style commands require. EPSV also does not force a NAT to rewrite the address inside the traffic, whereas EPRT would.

A client can send EPSV ALL to tell NATs that EPRT and the other data commands will no longer be used, so they may put the connection on a fast path. After it, the server MUST reject all data connection setup commands other than EPSV, including EPRT, PORT and PASV. A client that expects only two-way transfers SHOULD send it as soon as possible. If it later needs a three-way transfer, a new FTP session MUST be started.
sections.eli5: Telling the network that you will only ever ask the server to open doors, never the other way, lets the network helper stop watching your messages closely.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The authors do not believe these changes introduce new security problems. They point to a companion Work in Progress on FTP security considerations, which discusses FTP security issues and techniques to reduce them more generally.
sections.eli5: The authors think the new commands do not make FTP less safe, and another document covers FTP safety in general.
